title: A Tweet and the Raindrop
text:
I ran into this tweet yesterday:


Tweet by @mathelirium.

— (@mathelirium) April 27, 2026


In the simulations, we see the behavior of no viscosity \(\nu = 0\) and vanishing viscosity \(\nu \rightarrow 0\) are different, and not the second doesn’t converge to the first. This reminded me of a problem I solved back in high school, called The Raindrop.
The detailed statement and the solution of the problem can be found here.
Briefly, we consider a raindrop that falls down under the influence of gravity in a medium of that is filled with many small water droplets. The drop merges with the droplets as it moves, and grows. We simplify our model by considering the droplets as a medium of constant density \(\lambda \neq 0\) where the droplets are stationary. We denote the density of the raindrop as \(\rho\), and investigate the inelastic collisions between the raindrop and the droplets.
After solving a few short differential equations, we get the acceleration of the raindrop as \(a=g/7\). This result is surprising to me, because it does not depend on \(\rho\) or \(\lambda\). Even though it’s a nice result, this lack of dependence gives us a weird result in the edge cases of our problem: What happens if \(\lambda = 0\)? Physically, we expect to have \(a=g\), because there is nothing that’s slowing down the raindrop. Mathematically, the issue is easy to spot. In Eq. 5 of the solution, the ratio \(\rho/\lambda\) is not defined when \(\lambda = 0\). Therefore, the solution is not valid for that case. Thus, we can generalize our solution as \[\begin{align*}
a(\lambda) =
\begin{cases}
g, &\lambda = 0\\
g/7, &\lambda > 0
\end{cases}
\end{align*}\] Now, even though this is a mathematically complete solution, the fact that the \(\lambda > 0\) solution does not converge to the \(\lambda = 0\) solution makes me uncomfortable, in the same way the tweet I shared made me feel. At this point, of course, we need to revisit our problem setup and the physical model to see where things went wrong. First of all, we cannot model many small droplets as a medium of uniform density. Second, we cannot simplify the interactions of fluid masses by only considering inelastic collisions. If we push further, we can even find inconsistencies within the model itself: For one, I am not convinced that the raindrop would keep its spherical shape during its motion, even in this simplified model.
Therefore, what I conclude it that even though it is entertaining and insightful to obtain solutions for complex problems using oversimplified solution, it is not worth the time to think about the physically inconsistent results we get from these solutions. After all, neither the model nor the the solution is real, only our intutition is real. Of course, if there are almost no droplets but still some droplets, the raindrop will move with an acceleration closer to \(g\), and we don’t need a model to arrive to this conclusion.

title: End of my internship at LLR
text:
Yesterday, on June 30, I presented the results of my 5 month internship at the LHCb team of Laboratoire Leprince-Ringuet at the weekly simulation meeting of the LHCb collaboration of CERN.
This presentation marks the end of my internship, and I have mixed feelings. Needless to say, working on particle physics has been a dream as long as I can remember, and I feel proud to say I was a part of the researchers working at CERN. But it was also surprising in ways that I did not expect.
First of all, the particle physics phenomenology research has a completely different structure from what I experienced before. My previous intership was at the Irradiated Solids Laboratory of Polytechnique. Whether the work is hands-on experiments or running simulations on a computer, the structure was that you would find yourself an interesting question, and spend months trying to answer that with at most 5-10 people that you keep contact about the specific subject. For LLR, it was a lot different: There were people from literally all around the world, constantly emailing each other or giving presentations. Each team was focusing on a very small detail of a very small subsection of the entire experiment, and all these people were coming together to run the biggest man-made machine. The information was so structurally organized, and very neatly formatted. It was impossible for any work that is done by some team to be missed by another team and replicated. From what I’ve seen so far, this was the only real example of collaboration in research, and all the other research groups in other fields act as individuals compared to the particle physics people.
Second issue was the fact that my internship felt more like a programming internship than a physics one. I was sitting in the office all day, writing data analysis code and generating plots. As a matter of fact, the first few weeks of my internship was just me learning how to access the virtual machines and trying to remember to do bash everytime I logged in. I still don’t know why I need to do that… But to be honest, this issue would not be an issue if it wasn’t for the next thing I’m going to mention, which is the fact that I didn’t know particle physics.
Of course, it would be unreasonable to expect a second year undergraduate student to know particle physics to the point that they would understand everything they are doing. The researchers working on particle physics are aware of this. For that reason, whenever an undergraduate student arrives at their lab looking for an internship, they just tell the student that they do not need to understand everything, and that they would be just fine as long as they know some Python and how to ask stuff to ChatGPT. Is this a healty way of approaching to an internship? Well, there is not really any other option for the researchers. They can’t teach the student high energy physics theory in the time frame of “4 hours every week for 5 months”. Let alone teaching actual particle physics, they can’t even get through all of the prerequisites. At this point, however, I think the student should be able to make an informed decision. In my situation, I was a little lost in the excitement of working at CERN, and I didn’t really think much about what I would be learning from this internship. In the end, I can’t say I didn’t learn anything. I learned a lot about how the reserach worked, a lot of basic information about how the experiments are combined with simulations, how the simulated data is generated, etc. However, I can’t keep myself from thinking, would I have learned more if I did an internship that was more suitable for my level and skills? Probably yes…
With all these said, I genuinely think that this internship was a valuable experience for me. I think that it would be even more valuable if I had intentions of working in experimental particle physics in my later life. I have friends with such plans, and they absolute love the time they spend doing this kind of work. What I can suggest to people interested in this type of internship is that they should carefully think through what they want to do after they graduate, and choose their internships according to their goals. After all, one can fit only a few internships in their undergraduate education, especially if it’s three years long.
Anyways, the report from my intership and the presentation slides from the defense are below, in case anyone is interested in seeing how a research project in particle physics without knowing any particle physics looks.

title: Problem Sets
text:
I spent 5 years studying for physics olympiads back in high schools. In my school, like many other olympiad-oriented schools, if you were old enough, you would start tutoring the younger promotions. In most of my tutoring sessions, I would just solve the probems from textbooks or the problem sets our professor had prepared. In my last year, however, I took on a bigger responsibility and prepared 3 problem sets with selected problems from different souces after my professor asked for it.
Later, from September 2025 to February 2025, I tutored another student preparing for olympiads privately. I prepared 9 more problem sets for her for our sessions, this time increasing the variety of the souces I picked the problems from.
These 12 problem sets (first 3 in Turkish, rest in English) contains problems varying from introductory level to Olympiad level in almost all topics contained in the physics olympiads curriculum. They are not particularly original, but I think they would be useful for students trying to make sure there are no topics they didn’t cover, or to find new problem sources, since most problems have references to where they are from.
